overview: Kurs refers here to medieval Curonian communities around the eastern Baltic coast during 1000 to 1100, rather than a single kingdom. The imported outline covers western Latvia but omits southern Curonian lands in present-day Lithuania. Palanga’s excavated houses and objects, described below, are examples from that omitted southern region. Curonian culture developed across communities with different local histories.

periods.title: Medieval coastal communities
periods.summary: The mapped century falls within a period of settlement, trade and northward expansion into Finnic-inhabited areas.

items.text: During the eleventh century, Curonian influence spread north into areas inhabited by Baltic Finnic communities. Talsi and Mežīte were among the centres affected. This involved movement and cultural mixing, so the map’s single colour hides a more complicated human landscape.

Farming and livestock keeping supported the Curonian economy, alongside fishing, hunting and forest beekeeping. Seafaring was important, but meals still depended on work in fields, pastures, woods and waterways. A community of sailors also needed people who could grow and gather food.

Talsi hillfort had timber defences by the tenth century: a double wooden wall stood above packed stones, with houses arranged beside it. Excavations distinguish nine building phases across occupation lasting into the fourteenth century.

At Palanga, south of the map’s outline, a tenth- or eleventh-century log house burned with much of its contents inside. Archaeologists found a rectangular hearth beside the north wall, broken pots in the northeast kitchen corner and another hearth in a working area. The disaster preserved an unusually readable household plan.

An addition to the same Palanga house held a loom. When the building burned, its weights collapsed where the weaving equipment had stood. Those weights help identify a working space even though the wooden loom did not survive intact. Making cloth was a substantial household activity, visible through equipment left on the floor.

These houses came to light during work on a modern park’s sprinklers, drainage and lighting in 2010. Archaeologists tested the threatened ground and investigated exposed settlement layers. Windblown sand had covered the older remains. A trench for a modern pipe unexpectedly became a window into medieval domestic life.

A Palanga find identified as an ice skate was made from a horse’s lower leg bone. The municipal display also includes an iron point from a wooden pole. Such objects reveal a practical response to winter conditions: a useful animal bone could acquire a second career beneath a person’s foot.

The same display includes a stone gaming piece and a fragment tentatively identified as part of a chess piece. The second identification remains uncertain. These small objects suggest that life in a trading settlement included play as well as work, though the exact rules of a particular game may escape us.

A Palanga grave from the late tenth or early eleventh century held a woman and a girl. Their burial objects provide a glimpse of people often missing from accounts focused on warriors and ships. Being buried together does not by itself establish that they were mother and daughter.

Boat nails and rivets survive from Viking-period Palanga settlements. Small fastenings are valuable evidence where complete wooden boats have disappeared. They connect the coastal settlement’s archaeological record with the practical work of assembling and maintaining seagoing craft.

An eleventh-century silver-ingot hoard from Impiltis helps researchers reconstruct connections between Palanga and Grobiņa. Archaeologist Jonas Genys emphasises overland routes as well as waterways. Travelling goods could move through several hands and along several kinds of road before reaching their final owners.

Imported glass beads present an interesting detective problem. Genys notes that similar beads were made in western European centres as well as arriving through eastern networks. A colourful bead therefore cannot automatically be assigned a distant eastern origin. Shape, material and comparisons with excavated examples all matter.

Metalworkers obtained iron from local bog ore and fashioned tools and weapons. Smelting furnaces are known at centres including Talsi and Žardė. Turning muddy-looking ore into useful metal required specialised knowledge, another kind of achievement beside the battles recorded in chronicles.

sections.title: A language without a surviving sentence

items.text: Curonian belonged to the Baltic language family, but no surviving written monument supplies a secure medieval Curonian sentence for this card. Names, place names and traces in later languages provide evidence instead. Modern Lithuanian, Latvian and the later Kursenieki language should not be presented as exact quotations from an eleventh-century Curonian speaker.

ending.text: Curonian communities continued after 1100. Crusading conquest divided their lands between the Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order and the bishop of Courland in 1253. Resistance continued, and the peace imposed in 1267 completed the conquest. People remained, while political control and cultural identities changed over later centuries.
